articles.title: Experiential Retail: What Works Now and What Doesn’t
articles.narrative: The global experiential retail market, valued at $132 billion in 2025, is projected to more than quadruple by 2035 with a compound annual growth rate of 15.2 percent, driven by evolving consumer preferences among millennials and Gen Z for immersive and interactive shopping experiences. This shift moves beyond traditional transactional retail to focus on creating memorable, emotional connections and increasing dwell time and brand loyalty. Successful experiential retail development requires a fundamental change in approach, emphasizing storytelling, meticulous curation, and intentional design details to stand out in a competitive landscape where online shopping handles product exchanges. Developers must create destinations that offer layered and elevated experiences to make in-person visits worthwhile for consumers.

articles.title: A calmer U.S. industrial market? That’s what Colliers has found
articles.narrative: Colliers' latest U.S. industrial report indicates a stabilizing market where demand is now outpacing new supply, leading to a slight decrease in the national vacancy rate to 7.3% in Q2 2026. This marks a significant shift after two years of increasing vacancies, with 63% of tracked markets showing stable or declining rates. Leasing demand strengthened considerably, with net absorption nearly doubling year-over-year to 59 million square feet, predominantly in the South. New deliveries have slowed to their lowest quarterly total since 2016, helping to rebalance the market, though the construction pipeline is growing again, reaching 312 million square feet. Rental rates are also stabilizing, with average asking rents at $10.34 per square foot, reflecting modest corrections in some coastal markets.

articles.title: Housing Notes: Explaining the silver tsunami with surveys
articles.narrative: This article analyzes two seemingly contradictory surveys regarding Baby Boomer housing preferences: one by Freddie Mac suggesting most boomers plan to downsize, and another by NAR indicating boomers are buying larger homes. The author, a boomer who downsized, attributes the discrepancy to differing definitions of "downsizing" (e.g., square footage vs. maintenance burden) and the inherent unreliability of self-reported survey data versus actual transaction records. The piece concludes that while older boomers may sell smaller homes, many boomers are purchasing similar or larger properties, highlighting the limitations of surveys in capturing complex consumer behavior.

The fund's strategy aims to capitalize on opportunities in the private credit market, where non-bank lenders are increasingly active.
articles.market_intelligence: Private credit loans totaled $1.4 trillion in the second half of last year, indicating a significant market for non-bank lending.

articles.title: Policy Pro: City rejects buyer protections for pied-à-terre tax, Council seeks rental benefit boost
articles.narrative: New York City's Department of Finance has finalized rules for its pied-à-terre tax on luxury second homes, notably omitting an "innocent purchaser" provision that real estate attorneys advocated for. This means buyers could be liable for a previous owner's unpaid tax bill, with the city advising buyers to negotiate risk allocation with sellers. Separately, a City Council bill aims to expand eligibility for the Senior Citizens Rent Increase Exemption (SCRIE) and Disability Rent Increase Exemption (DRIE) programs by raising the income cap to $75,000 from $50,000, retroactively effective to July 1. This initiative seeks to enhance housing security for low-income residents and potentially reduce tenant turnover for landlords, though challenges remain in increasing program awareness and accessibility for eligible households.

articles.title: Buckling scare puts MetroLoft’s ‘scoop-and-stack’ playbook under microscope
articles.narrative: A structural failure at MetroLoft's conversion of Pfizer's former Midtown headquarters at 235 East 42nd Street in New York City has drawn attention to the developer's "scoop-and-stack" redevelopment technique. This method involves hollowing out lower floors to create lightwells and transferring development potential to new floors added at the top, addressing the challenge of deep floor plates in postwar office-to-residential conversions. While the incident is under investigation, the developer attributed the buckling to insufficiently reinforced columns rather than a flaw in the overall concept, with missing reinforcing steel plates identified as a potential cause.

articles.title: New dev deals sink as Manhattan luxury contends with shrinking pipeline

This decline is attributed to a shrinking new development pipeline, which has led to a 62 percent reduction in new construction inventory over the past year. Despite the drop in new development supply, the broader Manhattan luxury market still saw 27 signed deals for homes asking $4 million or more in mid-July, totaling $205 million, with an average price of $7.6 million.

articles.title: Miami is now more expensive than New York City
articles.article_type: Market Research / Cost of Living Report
articles.narrative: A new report indicates that the cost of living in the Miami metropolitan area has surpassed that of New York City for the first time on record, driven by significant increases in insurance costs, private school tuition, and restaurant spending. Since 2019, South Florida's consumer price index has surged by 36 percent, making it the second most expensive metro area nationally on the regional price parity index. While the absence of state income tax in Florida might seem appealing, other rising costs, particularly property taxes and the nation's highest home insurance premiums due to hurricane and flood risks, are eroding any savings for residents. This trend is occurring despite Miami's average household income being lower than the national median, creating a challenging environment for many residents.

articles.narrative: HarbourVest Partners, a global private markets investment firm, has secured its first New York City office with a 10-year lease for 19,752 square feet on the 49th floor of 9 West 57th Street. The move signifies a strategic expansion for the Boston-headquartered firm, which manages over $160 billion in assets. The selection of this prestigious building reflects HarbourVest's desire for a high-caliber space that offers an exceptional experience for both clients and employees, according to the tenant's broker.

articles.title: The $70B Quantum Boom Is Building A New Real Estate Sector
articles.narrative: A new real estate sector is emerging to support the $70 billion global investment in quantum computing, distinct from the artificial intelligence boom. This "quantum real estate" includes research labs, data centers, and fabrication sites, with over 240 facilities worldwide and a $4 billion construction pipeline. Unlike traditional data centers, early quantum facilities are concentrated in educational hubs like Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles, and San Francisco, prioritizing access to researchers and "quantum ecosystems" over cheap electricity. JLL projects that commercial quantum advantage will emerge between 2030 and 2032, with the quantum computing facilities market eventually reaching about 5% of the total data center market.

articles.title: How Merritt Properties' New CEO Plans To Deploy $750M Investment
articles.narrative: Merritt Properties, an industrial developer, secured a $750 million capital injection from longtime partner Almanac Realty Investors and new investor Centerbridge Partners. This investment, which gives the investors a 35% stake in the firm, will primarily fund new construction of shallow-bay industrial spaces, a segment of the market characterized by strong demand and undersupply. The company plans to focus its expansion in the Southeast, targeting markets with robust business growth, and will prioritize projects designed for tenants seeking smaller footprints.

data_points.notable_features: Focus on shallow-bay industrial spaces, typically 90-100 feet deep, for tenants seeking 9,000 SF or less.
data_points.project_notes: The initial investment was $500 million, with Centerbridge providing 73% and Almanac 27%. An additional $250 million is committed for future growth.

articles.market_intelligence: Shallow-bay industrial vacancy nationwide was 4.8% last quarter, compared to 6.9% for industrial overall. Overall industrial vacancy nationwide saw a 20-basis-point decline year-over-year in Q2. Vacancy for warehouses 750,000 SF and larger fell from 8.3% to 7.3% in the year leading up to Q2 2026.

articles.title: Controlled Turbulence Or Chaos? CBRE's Spencer Levy Checks In On 2026
articles.narrative: CBRE Global Client Strategist Spencer Levy believes the commercial real estate industry is largely on track with his earlier prediction of "controlled turbulence" for 2026, despite a Bisnow survey showing industry leaders are divided on market sentiment. Levy notes that while macro noise persists, particularly post-pandemic, the real estate sector has adapted to interest rate changes. This adaptation includes strategic shifts by major investors, who are reallocating capital to core-plus or value-add assets due to challenges in raising funds for core properties where returns are comparable to bonds but with higher risk. Levy also dismisses concerns about an impending "wall of maturities," stating that no reckoning is coming.

articles.title: Oceanwide Plaza Sale Primed To Move Forward
articles.narrative: A bankruptcy judge has indicated approval for the sale of the unfinished Oceanwide Plaza in Downtown Los Angeles, paving the way for the long-stalled $1.2 billion project to finally move forward. The city of Los Angeles withdrew its objections after provisions were added to the liquidation plan, requiring the proposed buyer, KPC Square LLC, to address blight and graffiti within 90 days and close the sale within six months. This development increases the likelihood of the prominent mixed-use development reaching substantial completion after sitting dormant for over six years.

data_points.notable_features: Incomplete mixed-use development that has been stalled for over six years.
data_points.project_notes: The sale is part of a liquidation plan in bankruptcy court. The buyer is required to initiate graffiti removal and blight abatement within 90 days and close the sale within six months, with potential for extension by unanimous agreement.

articles.title: Chicago Ranks No. 3 For AI Job Growth As Office Market Stands To Benefit
articles.narrative: Chicago is emerging as a significant hub for artificial intelligence job growth, ranking third nationally behind New York City and San Francisco in year-over-year increases in AI-related job postings. This surge, with nearly 10,000 new postings, is driven by demand across diverse sectors including medical, finance, and education, not just traditional tech companies. While AI companies' national office footprint has grown to 9.2M SF, and 308K SF in Chicago, the direct impact of this hiring boom on office leasing trends in Chicago remains uncertain, as companies are not yet translating AI job growth into a one-to-one increase in office space demand.
